lead: When a gas dissolves in a liquid that also reacts with it, the liquid film near the interface carries diffusion and reaction together. The reaction eats the dissolved gas, keeps the interfacial gradient steep, and pushes the flux above the physical value. The ratio is the enhancement factor E. The Hatta number Ha compares reaction speed with diffusion speed and decides the regime. CO₂ scrubbing with amine and H₂S scrubbing with alkali depend on this effect.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.4 for the film picture and kL, Chapter 2.6 for film resistances and interface equilibrium, and first-order kinetics.

sections.h3: Reaction inside the film steepens the gradient

blocks.text: Start with physical absorption. Gas A dissolves at the interface at C<sub>Ai</sub> and diffuses through a liquid film of thickness δ into the bulk at C<sub>Ab</sub>. The flux is N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>L</sub>(C<sub>Ai</sub> − C<sub>Ab</sub>), with N<sub>A</sub> in mol/(m²·s), k<sub>L</sub> in m/s and C in mol/m³. The profile is a straight line, and the flux equals D<sub>A</sub> times the slope at the interface.

Now let A react first order in the liquid, rate = k·C<sub>A</sub> with k in s⁻¹. Inside the film A is removed by reaction as well as diffusion. The profile sags below the straight line and can reach zero before the film edge (figure). The flux is still N<sub>A</sub> = −D<sub>A</sub>(dC<sub>A</sub>/dx) at x = 0, so a steeper starting slope means a bigger flux.
E = N<sub>A</sub> with reaction ÷ N<sub>A</sub> without reaction   (same C<sub>Ai</sub>, same k<sub>L</sub>)
blocks.where: E is the enhancement factor, dimensionless and ≥ 1; N<sub>A</sub> is the molar flux of A in mol/(m²·s); both fluxes are taken at the same interfacial concentration and the same physical k<sub>L</sub>.

blocks.text: Keep two effects apart. Reaction inside the film raises E. Reaction in the bulk lowers C<sub>Ab</sub> towards zero, which protects the driving force (C<sub>Ai</sub> − C<sub>Ab</sub>) but does not raise E. A slow reaction gives E ≈ 1 and still helps by keeping the driving force at its maximum.

sections.h3: The Hatta number sorts the regimes

blocks.where: Ha is the Hatta number (dimensionless); k is the first-order rate constant in s⁻¹; D<sub>A</sub> is the liquid diffusivity of A in m²/s; k<sub>L</sub> is the physical liquid film coefficient in m/s, the value you would have with no reaction.

blocks.text: The film thickness is roughly δ = D<sub>A</sub>/k<sub>L</sub>, so Ha ≈ √(k·δ²/D<sub>A</sub>) = δ ÷ √(D<sub>A</sub>/k). The length √(D<sub>A</sub>/k) is the distance A travels before it reacts. Ha measures film thickness in units of that length. Big Ha means the reaction wins.

blocks.where: E is the enhancement factor for a first-order reaction in the film; tanh is the hyperbolic tangent. For Ha > 3, tanh(Ha) ≈ 1 and E ≈ Ha. For Ha < 0.3, tanh(Ha) ≈ Ha and E ≈ 1.

blocks.text: The fast pseudo-first-order result needs 3 < Ha << E∞. As Ha approaches E∞, a reaction plane forms and E saturates at E∞ = 1 + (D<sub>B</sub>·C<sub>B</sub>)/(b·D<sub>A</sub>·C<sub>Ai</sub>), where C<sub>B</sub> is bulk concentration of B in mol/m³, D<sub>B</sub> its liquid diffusivity in m²/s, and b the moles of B per mole of A. More B or faster diffusion of B is the only help.

sections.h3: Where it is used: reactive absorption

blocks.text: Carbon dioxide scrubbing with aqueous monoethanolamine (MEA) is the standard example. The reaction is second order, but with the amine in large excess it behaves as pseudo-first order with k = k<sub>2</sub>C<sub>MEA</sub>. With k<sub>2</sub> of a few thousand m³/(kmol·s) at 25 °C and a few kmol/m³ of amine, k is of order 10⁴ s⁻¹, and with D<sub>A</sub> near 1.5×10⁻⁹ m²/s and k<sub>L</sub> near 10⁻⁴ m/s, Ha comes out at several tens. Then E ≈ Ha, and the liquid-film resistance drops from 1/k<sub>L</sub> to 1/(E·k<sub>L</sub>). The tower height falls by about E only when the liquid film controls; with a strong gas-film resistance the height hardly changes.

Hydrogen sulphide in dilute caustic soda behaves differently. The proton transfer is essentially instantaneous, so the column runs at E∞, limited by how fast OH⁻ diffuses to the reaction plane. Fresh caustic enters at the top and loads on the way down; near the bottom, where B is lowest and the gas richest, E∞ falls.

items: Design flux: N<sub>A</sub> = E·k<sub>L</sub>·C<sub>Ai</sub>, valid only when C<sub>Ab</sub> ≈ 0 (fast regime).
kL must be the physical coefficient from a correlation (Chapter 2.3), never back-calculated from an experiment with reaction.
Raising liquid rate raises k<sub>L</sub>, lowers Ha and lowers E. Each extra unit of pumping buys less than one unit of flux.
Interfacial CAi comes from Henry's law and gas-side resistance (Chapter 2.6).

figure.caption: Film-theory profiles of dissolved A for a first-order reaction, C<sub>A</sub>/C<sub>Ai</sub> = sinh[Ha(1 − x/δ)]/sinh Ha with no A in the bulk. Without reaction the profile is straight; at Ha = 1 it sags and the wall slope, which sets the flux, is 1.31 times steeper; at the example's Ha = 14.1 the A is used up within a tenth of the film and the flux is 14.1 times the physical value.

spec.aria: Plot of dissolved A concentration over its interface value against distance into the liquid film: a dashed straight line for no reaction, a sagging curve for Hatta number 1, and a curve for Hatta number 14.1 that falls to near zero within the first tenth of the film, with its steep tangent at the interface. A panel lists the example data and the fluxes 5.0e-7 and 7.07e-6 mol per square metre per second.

examples.question: A gas A dissolves in a liquid in which it undergoes a first-order reaction with rate constant k = 10 s⁻¹. The liquid diffusivity of A is D<sub>A</sub> = 2×10⁻⁹ m²/s and the physical liquid-film coefficient is k<sub>L</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s. The interfacial concentration is C<sub>Ai</sub> = 0.05 mol/m³ and the bulk concentration of A is negligible. (a) Find the Hatta number. (b) Name the regime and find the enhancement factor. (c) Find the flux with and without reaction.
examples.answer: Ha = 14.14, the reaction is fast pseudo-first-order, E = 14.14, and the flux rises from 5.0×10⁻⁷ to 7.07×10⁻⁶ mol/(m²·s).
examples.check:
import math
k = 10.0
D = 2e-9
kL = 1.0e-5
CAi = 0.05
Ha = math.sqrt(k*D)/kL
E = Ha/math.tanh(Ha)
N0 = kL*CAi
N = E*N0
print(round(Ha, 2))
print(round(E, 2))
print(round(N0, 10))
print(round(N, 8))

traps: Using the gas-side coefficient in Ha. k<sub>L</sub> and D<sub>A</sub> are liquid-side values; putting k<sub>G</sub> or a gas diffusivity gives a meaningless number.

Unit slips: k in s⁻¹, D<sub>A</sub> in m²/s, k<sub>L</sub> in m/s. Mixing cm²/s with m/s shifts Ha by a factor of 100, because 1 cm²/s = 10⁻⁴ m²/s and the square root halves that power of ten. A factor of 100 can flip the regime.
Quoting E ≈ Ha everywhere. It holds only for 3 < Ha << E∞; below use E = Ha/tanh(Ha); at the limit use E∞ = 1 + (D<sub>B</sub>·C<sub>B</sub>)/(b·D<sub>A</sub>·C<sub>Ai</sub>).
Treating E as a ratio of measured k<sub>L</sub> values from two runs. E is a flux ratio at the same C<sub>Ai</sub> and physical k<sub>L</sub>.
Thinking a slow reaction is useless because E ≈ 1. It keeps C<sub>Ab</sub> near zero, so the full driving force survives — a bulk effect, not film enhancement.

quiz.q: Define the enhancement factor E for absorption with chemical reaction.
quiz.a: E = flux of A with reaction ÷ flux of A without reaction, compared at the same interfacial concentration C<sub>Ai</sub> and the same physical liquid film coefficient k<sub>L</sub>. It is dimensionless and at least 1.

quiz.q: Write the Hatta number for a first-order reaction and give the SI units of each symbol.
quiz.a: Ha = √(k·D<sub>A</sub>)/k<sub>L</sub>, where k is in s⁻¹, D<sub>A</sub> in m²/s and k<sub>L</sub> in m/s. Ha is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does a fast reaction increase the flux even though the interfacial concentration is unchanged?
quiz.a: The reaction removes A inside the film, so the concentration falls steeply just inside the interface instead of following a straight line. The flux equals D<sub>A</sub> times the slope at x = 0, so a steeper slope gives a larger flux.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction has k = 100 s⁻¹ in a liquid with D<sub>A</sub> = 1×10⁻⁹ m²/s. The physical k<sub>L</sub> is 2×10⁻⁵ m/s. Find Ha and E, and name the regime.
quiz.a: k·D<sub>A</sub> = 1×10⁻⁷ m²/s²; √ = 3.162×10⁻⁴ m/s; Ha = 3.162×10⁻⁴ ÷ 2×10⁻⁵ = 15.8. Since Ha > 3, the regime is fast pseudo-first-order and E ≈ Ha = 15.8.

quiz.q: The liquid flow rate in a packed absorber is doubled. State what happens to k<sub>L</sub>, Ha and E, and why the flux does not double.
quiz.a: Higher liquid rate raises k<sub>L</sub>. Since Ha = √(k·D<sub>A</sub>)/k<sub>L</sub>, Ha falls; in the fast regime E ≈ Ha, so E falls too. The flux N = E·k<sub>L</sub>·C<sub>Ai</sub> changes only as √(k·D<sub>A</sub>) in this regime, so it becomes nearly independent of liquid rate — the gain from more pumping shrinks.

quiz.q: In the instantaneous regime, E stops depending on the rate constant k. Explain why, and say what it depends on instead.
quiz.a: When the reaction is fast enough, A and B cannot coexist; they meet at a plane and both are consumed there. The process is limited by diffusion of A and B to that plane, not by reaction speed. E becomes E∞ = 1 + (D<sub>B</sub>·C<sub>B</sub>)/(b·D<sub>A</sub>·C<sub>Ai</sub>), set by diffusivities, the bulk concentration of B and the stoichiometry b.

quiz.q: A reaction gives E = 1.02. Is it worth adding to the solvent?
quiz.a: Yes, for a different reason. The enhancement is negligible, but the reaction holds the bulk concentration of A near zero, so the driving force stays at C<sub>Ai</sub> all the way down the column instead of building up. This is how slow-reacting solvents are used.

beyond: Not for the exam. Reactive absorption is the front end of most CO₂ capture plants; amine scrubbing, hot potassium carbonate and chilled ammonia trade reaction rate against regeneration energy. Membrane contactors put the same film physics inside hollow fibres. Reactive distillation runs reaction and separation in one column, with Ha still deciding film or bulk. For enzymes, the Michaelis–Menten rate replaces k·C<sub>A</sub>. Search: reactive absorption enhancement factor, Hatta number CO₂ MEA, gas–liquid reactor design.
